passage:
Monday: Anirban told Jeevan Sir why his homework was late, and Sir tilted his head. Anirban thought, He's listening and he's sorry for me, and he explained the whole story.
Wednesday: Anirban said he had finished all the sums. Sir tilted his head again and said nothing. Anirban's stomach clenched: Does he think I'm lying? “Show me your working for number seven,” said Sir, in an easy voice. Anirban showed him, and Sir nodded.
Friday: Anirban watched Sir tilt his head at a friend. Sir's eyes were warm. “Tell me more,” he said. Anirban smiled a little. The tilt was the same, but the tone told him more.

qa.q: What did Jeevan Sir ask Anirban to show him on Wednesday?
qa.a: He asked him to show his working for number seven.

qa.q: What did Anirban think Sir's head tilt meant on Monday and on Wednesday?
qa.a: On Monday he read it as listening and sympathy, so he explained everything. On Wednesday he read it as doubt and his stomach clenched, though Sir may just have been curious.

qa.q: What could Anirban do when he is not sure what a head tilt means?
qa.a: Notice the tone and face that come with it, and ask a question if he is unsure, like “Is something wrong with my answer?”

qa.q: How might Jeevan Sir see his own head tilt?
qa.a: Probably as a sign that he is listening and thinking, without realising it can look like doubt to a nervous child.

grounding: A head tilt can show curiosity, sympathy or doubt; tone and body add the meaning.

passage:
“When I was ten,” said Gautam Nana, “my teacher Mrs Pillai tilted her head when I said I had not copied Ramesh's sum. My heart sank. I thought, She doesn't believe me. I stood there stiff as a post.”
“What happened?” asked Jaya.
“She said, in a kind voice, ‘Tell me how you got it.’ I showed her my working and her face cleared. The tilt was only because she wanted to hear more.” He smiled. “Now when a teacher tilts her head I remember the tone. It can be curiosity, or sympathy, or doubt. You have to look at the whole face.”

qa.q: Who tilted her head when Gautam said he had not copied?
qa.a: Mrs Pillai tilted her head.

qa.q: What did young Gautam think the head tilt meant, and what did it turn out to be?
qa.a: He thought Mrs Pillai did not believe him and felt worried and upset, since his heart sank and he stood stiff. It turned out she only wanted to hear more.

qa.q: What could Jaya learn from Nana's story?
qa.a: That a head tilt has several possible meanings, so she should look at the whole face and tone, and offer her working or explanation.

qa.q: How might Mrs Pillai have seen Gautam's stiff face?
qa.a: Probably as worry, and she did not intend doubt. Her kind “Tell me how you got it” suggests she wanted to put him at ease.

grounding: A head tilt in a teacher may be curiosity, sympathy or doubt; tone and the whole face add meaning.

passage: The bell was about to ring, and the corridor was jammed with Class 7 pushing past. Kunal had one minute to explain to Karthik Sir why his project was late. “My printer ran out of ink, and the shop was shut, so I…” Sir tilted his head to one side. Kunal's words tangled. He doesn't believe me. Then he noticed Sir had also leaned closer, one hand cupped near his ear, eyebrows soft. “Say that again? It's so noisy.” Kunal almost laughed. The tilt was for hearing. He repeated it, louder. Sir nodded. “Bring it tomorrow. Thanks for telling me.”

qa.q: Why was Kunal's project late?
qa.a: His printer ran out of ink, and the shop was shut.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when Sir tilted his head?
qa.a: Kunal felt anxious and doubted, thinking the tilt meant Sir didn't believe him.

qa.q: What cues helped Kunal read the tilt correctly?
qa.a: Sir's leaning closer, the cupped hand near his ear and his soft eyebrows showed he was trying to hear, not doubting.

qa.q: What was the moment like for Karthik Sir?
qa.a: Sir was struggling to hear over the noisy corridor and just wanted Kunal to repeat himself.

grounding: Shows a child reading a teacher's head tilt as doubt, when body cues and tone show listening.

passage: In their Delhi flat, Mridul came out of his room and announced, “Mumma, room's all clean.” Anjali looked up from her laptop and tilted her head to one side. Mridul smiled. She's impressed. Then he noticed the rest: one eyebrow lifted, lips pressed into a small line, and her voice, slow and flat. “Oh, really? All clean?” He shifted his feet. His cricket kit was still on the bed, and the socks were under it. “Mostly clean,” he said. Anjali's head straightened and she laughed. “Mostly. Go finish, and then I'll come and see.”

qa.q: What was still on Mridul's bed?
qa.a: His cricket kit was still on the bed.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling when he first saw the head tilt?
qa.a: He felt pleased and hopeful, thinking she was impressed, before the other cues made him uneasy.

qa.q: Which cues told Mridul the tilt meant doubt?
qa.a: The lifted eyebrow, pressed lips and slow, flat voice showed that the tilt meant doubt, not admiration.

qa.q: How did Anjali see Mridul's announcement?
qa.a: Anjali doubted the room was really clean and used a teasing tone to let him admit it himself.

grounding: Shows a child reading a parent's head tilt, first as interest, then as doubt once the eyebrow and tone are added.

passage: “And then they changed the group chat name so I wasn't in it anymore.” Ankita stopped. Sarita Ma'am had tilted her head to one side. “You don't believe me,” Ankita said quickly. “Why do you say that?” “Your head. My tuition teacher does that when she thinks I'm making excuses.” “Ah.” Sarita Ma'am kept her voice low and warm. “For me it means I'm listening hard. It sounds like that really hurt.” Ankita looked at her face again: soft eyes, no frown, leaning in. “It did.” “Thank you for telling me. Let's work out together what we can do about it today.”

qa.q: What did the group change so Ankita wasn't in it?
qa.a: They changed the group chat name so Ankita wasn't in it anymore.

qa.q: Why did Ankita think Sarita Ma'am didn't believe her?
qa.a: Ankita felt anxious and defensive, because her tuition teacher tilts her head like that when she doubts excuses.

qa.q: What helped Ankita read the tilt differently?
qa.a: Sarita Ma'am explained what the tilt meant for her, and her soft eyes, warm voice and leaning in backed it up.

qa.q: What was Sarita Ma'am trying to show with the tilt?
qa.a: She was trying to show she was listening closely and felt sympathy for how hurt Ankita was.

grounding: Shows a child reading a teacher's head tilt as doubt, when tone and body show sympathy and listening.

passage: I'm Uday. Last year I worked out that Ganga Ma'am's head tilt had at least three meanings. When I told her I'd opened up my grandfather's old radio, her head tilted, her eyebrows went up and she said, "Really? Then what?" That was curiosity. When I told her our cat had died, her head tilted the same way, but her voice went soft and she touched my shoulder. That was sympathy. And when I said the area was "forty metres", she tilted her head, pressed her lips together and said, "Hmm. Are you sure?" That one was doubt. I checked. It was forty square metres. The tilt was the same; the rest of her told me which one.

qa.q: What was the correct answer to the area question?
qa.a: Forty square metres.

qa.q: What was Ganga Ma'am most likely feeling when her head tilted and her voice went soft?
qa.a: Sympathy and some sadness for Uday about the cat, shown by the soft voice and the touch on the shoulder.

qa.q: What can Uday do when a teacher's head tilt is hard to read?
qa.a: Look at the rest of the face and voice, the eyebrows, lips and words, and if it is still unclear, simply ask.

qa.q: What would change if Uday judged the tilt alone, without the voice and face?
qa.a: Uday could mistake doubt for curiosity and miss the hint to check the answer, or take sympathy for doubt.

grounding: It is a child's account of reading a teacher's head tilt as curiosity, sympathy or doubt depending on the face, tone and words around it.
